extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and readers of political science; analysts of political leadership and party systems
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and assess the qualities, roles, and institutional effects that produce different kinds of statesmen in democratic party systems (with emphasis on the United States vs. Europe). Useful for judging political leaders' suitability for foreign policy, legislation, administration, parliamentary management, or mass leadership.

rubrics_metrics.name: American temperament: cool, sober yet excitable
rubrics_metrics.description: The American is 'shrewd and keen, his passion seldom obscures his reason; he keeps his head' yet is 'of an excitable temper, with emotions capable of being quickly and strongly stirred.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains how Americans can remain rational in crises while also being rapidly mobilized into strong collective enthusiasm; illustrated by comparison with Scotch, French, Italian, and German temperaments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for excitement and competition
rubrics_metrics.description: Americans 'like excitement. They like it for its own sake, and go wherever they can find it' and take delight in forms of competition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This taste for excitement and rivalry helps explain intense popular involvement in presidential elections and other contests which may be entered into with only limited engagement with substantive issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitivity to size and mass ('A big thing')
rubrics_metrics.description: The American imagination is 'peculiarly sensitive to the impression of great size'—'A big thing' is a habitual phrase of admiration; the lateral extension of an idea (its mass) moves Americans more than its profundity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leaders and movements that appear to animate millions will provoke disproportionate enthusiasm even if their ideas are not deep; evaluators must account for scale-driven appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstration and display culture
rubrics_metrics.description: Americans relish parades, badges, brass bands, triumphal arches and public demonstrations as a relief from everyday monotony and as expressions of equality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of a pervasive sentiment of equality, elites often join popular processions rather than sneer; visible displays are therefore effective means of signaling participation and rallying support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five European types of statesmen (roles needed in old countries)
rubrics_metrics.description: In countries like England, France, Germany, and Italy five sorts of statesmen are needed: (1) managers of foreign and colonial policy/diplomats, (2) constructive legislators/reformers, (3) administrators who manage departments, (4) parliamentary tacticians who understand men and form cabinets, and (5) leaders of the masses who watch and rouse public feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes which roles require eloquence (chiefly the mass leader) and gives examples (e.g., Lord Palmerston as tactician). Use these role-types as a checklist when assessing whether a polity has suitable leaders for each sphere.

rubrics_metrics.name: American dominant types: 'man of the desk' and 'man of the stump'
rubrics_metrics.description: American politics chiefly produces two types: (a) the man of the desk or legislature (shrewd, businesslike, administrative) and (b) the man of the convention and the stump (orator and organizer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These correspond roughly to European parliamentary tactician and leader-of-masses but take distinct American forms because of size of electorate and party organization; assess candidates against which sub-type is required for the office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traits of the 'man of the desk' (legislator/administrator)
rubrics_metrics.description: Usually shrewd, cool, hard-headed, often a practising counsel or attorney, with a 'tight grip of facts, a keen insight into men,' tact, resolute tenacity, readiness as an effective (rather than polished) speaker, and administrative skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such men often rise via local government, governorships, or state legislatures; they are valuable for internal development and administrative governance and are commonly found in the Senate. They may lack imaginative breadth or high eloquence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traits of the 'man of the stump' (convention/orator/intriguer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Requires gifts of oratory, fluency, command of sonorous rhetoric, humour, quick retort, a powerful voice, a forcible personality, and talents for intrigue and committee-room manipulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This type excels on the stump and in conventions (public stage) and in private caucuses (committee-room); evaluators should look for both public speaking skills and ability to manage party machinery and patronage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnetism as a decisive quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Magnetism—a genial manner, winning address, and personal charm—is 'among the highest qualities' a popular American leader can possess and 'immensely enhances' his powers both with masses and in backstairs politics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Magnetism can substitute for other merits in popular leadership and is a central criterion for assessing popular electability and informal influence within parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intrigue and committee-room skill as a route to power
rubrics_metrics.description: Skill in manipulating bosses, rings, promises, vanity, and patronage—'to know their weaknesses, their ambitions, their jealousies'—secures advancement under the party system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluators should assess candidates' networks, capacity to form combinations, use of patronage, and reputation as 'good mixers'—these organizational skills often determine real influence irrespective of public talents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations imposed by the party system on high statesmanship
rubrics_metrics.description: The party system, through practices of intrigue, patronage, and convention-politics, is 'unfavourable to the development of the finest gifts'—narrowing men's minds, distorting vision, and making stump-habits unfit for guiding legislatures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging political systems or leaders, account for institutional incentives that promote committee-room skill and oratory over constructive, wide-ranging statesmanship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional/institutional constraints on national leadership
rubrics_metrics.description: Features like the disconnection of Congress from the executive and the existence of powerful States with their own party organizations mean leaders can rise by state-level success or boss-control without demonstrating national capacities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a candidate's career (state boss, ward-machine) reflects genuine national aptitude or merely the ability to deliver state/ward votes; compare to historical analogues (borough-monger).

rubrics_metrics.name: Public opinion is strong and often wholesome despite visible evils
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrary to some European impressions, 'public opinion is stronger or more active' in the United States and 'on the whole wholesome and upright,' even if political machinery shows dark lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysts should not equate visible party corruption with general moral failure of the electorate; consider the channels and organs through which opinion speaks before judging societal character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corruption often hidden; citizens see little and are heedless (lassitude)
rubrics_metrics.description: Much venality (especially in private legislation and closed-door committee work) is unseen by the populace; the habit of hearing accusations without careful probing makes citizens 'heedless' and places them in an intermediate state between belief and disbelief, producing lassitude rather than callousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations of civic virtue must account for information asymmetries, partisan press dynamics, and weak public visibility of legislative malfeasance; remedies focus on transparency and public scrutiny.
